title: First strategy: read the hand, not the last win
subtitle: 2 introductions · 5 practice · 5 independent tasks

theory.text: Use your current hand and the dealer upcard, not the previous round's win or loss. In our 6D/S17/DAS/late-surrender/peek/3:2 profile, hard 5–8 always Hit; hard 17–20 Stand. These boundaries remain the same against a small card or an ace. For example, 3+5 against 6 needs Hit, but 10+7 against 10 needs Stand. A strong dealer card does not mean you should always draw, and a good action can still lose. This first lesson focuses on hard hands without a splittable pair; soft hands, doubles and pairs follow separately. Try two guided examples, then ten scored decisions. Correct a mistake to continue, but the first answer remains the score.

theory.text: Keep the hand fixed and change only the dealer upcard. It often changes the best action, but the groups are not absolute. With hard 12, Stand against 4–6; Hit against 2–3 and 7–A. With hard 13–14, Stand against 2–6 and Hit against 7–A. Hard 8 still Hits a small card, while hard 17 still Stands against an ace. Compare 10+2 against 3 (Hit) and against 4 (Stand). Do not imagine that the dealer's hidden card is always ten; this is a reference strategy for the stated six-deck rules, not a prediction of one round. Practise recognizing the boundary before memorizing more totals.

theory.text: Double takes exactly one more card and ends the hand, so a small total alone is not enough. In our six-deck S17 profile, hard 9 doubles against 3–6; hard 10 against 2–9; hard 11 against 2–10, but Hits against an ace. Outside each range choose Hit. Double is available only on the first two cards here: after an extra card, the fallback for hard 9–11 is Hit, not Stand. Compare 5+6 against 6 (Double), 5+6 against A (Hit), and 2+3+6 against 6 (Hit because Double is unavailable). Follow the dealer boundary and the actual controls; do not transfer these rules automatically to H17 or another profile.

theory.text: These are hard hands, not pairs of eights. Against 2–6, Stand on hard 13–16. Against 7–A, usually Hit, with precise late-surrender exceptions: original two-card hard 15 against 10, and hard 16 against 9, 10 or A. Surrender is considered only after the dealer's blackjack check in our 6D/S17/DAS/late-surrender/peek/3:2 profile. After an extra card, Surrender is unavailable and those exceptions become Hit. Compare 10+6 against 6 (Stand), against 10 (Surrender), and 4+6+6 against 10 (Hit). A pair of eights with Split available is a different case: do not apply the hard-16 surrender shortcut to it. The decision is about the better average continuation, not predicting the next card.

coaching.contrast: Compare hard 15 vs 9 → Hit with 15 vs 10 → Surrender on two cards; 2+3+10 vs 10 → Hit after an extra card.

mistakes.hit: An extra card is not always the best continuation. Check the hand's exact row, the upcard, and whether Double or Split is available.
mistakes.stand: Standing is not always enough. Do not confuse the dealer's S17 rule with player strategy or transfer one pair's rule to another.
mistakes.doubleDown: Double means exactly one card and stopping. Check the upcard range; for a pair, check Split first.
mistakes.split: Equal values make Split available, not compulsory. Ten-value pairs stand, and nines have exceptions against 7, 10 and A.
mistakes.surrender: Surrender has exact original-hand 15/16 exceptions; it is not general risk avoidance. Splittable eights take Split first, and Surrender is unavailable after a split.

title: Core pairs: Split is not automatic
subtitle: 2 introductions · 5 practice · 5 independent tasks

theory.text: Our standard profile allows Split for two cards of equal value, including 10+K, up to four hands. Availability is not a recommendation. Split aces and eights against any upcard. Each split hand starts from one card of the pair and receives a new card. Aces receive only one card each and stop; 21 after Split is not natural blackjack. With other pairs, DAS allows Double on the new two-card hand, but Surrender is unavailable. After one 8+8 example, decide what to do with the resulting 8+3 hand. Smaller DAS-dependent pairs follow in the next lesson.

theory.text: In the standard six-deck S17 profile, Double After Split (DAS) allows doubling a new two-card hand after a non-ace split. Split 2s and 3s against 2–7, 4s against 5–6, 6s against 2–6, and 7s against 2–7. Otherwise Hit on these pairs. Treat 5+5 as hard 10: Double against 2–9, otherwise Hit; do not Split it. These are DAS rules, not a chart for a different profile. For example, 4+4 against 6 splits; a resulting 4+5 against 6 doubles. Split does not choose the next action for you: evaluate each new hand again. Split aces receive one card and stop. No result of a simulated wager is scored.

subtitle: 2 introductions · 5 practice · 5 independent tasks

theory.text: First read the available controls. An unavailable action cannot be the answer. After a third card, Double and Surrender are unavailable. Replace Double with Hit on hard 9–11 and soft 13–17, but with Stand on soft 18 against 3–6. If Split is unavailable, evaluate the pair as an ordinary hard or soft hand. For 8+8 against 10 this means Surrender if allowed, otherwise Hit; against 6 it means Stand. Two tasks explicitly disable an action just to practise this fallback: they are control-availability exercises, not a new casino rule profile. Actual hands after Split cannot Surrender, and at the four-hand limit cannot Split again. Late Surrender on an original hard 15 against 10 or hard 16 against 9, 10 or A applies only after the dealer peek. Do not confuse an unavailable choice with a bad enabled choice.
